name: Priya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for tech companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, and your name won't be attached.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to help. I'll warn you, I've got opinions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ashby's, a family farm with about four thousand free-range hens in mobile sheds, plus oilseed rape and wheat. Carol Ashby runs it with her husband. My day starts at six, opening the pop holes, then egg collection, grading and packing for the shops and the wholesaler. In the afternoon I move the sheds with the telehandler, check the birds, and in harvest I help with carting grain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology come into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the one who set up the AI assistant for the egg orders and invoices, because Carol was doing it all on paper at midnight. I use it every day, for orders, for checking the flock records, for everything. The pay's low and I rent a room from my aunt in the village, with about a fortnight's money saved. But I want my own egg business one day, a mobile shed of my own on rented ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so the AI assistant stays as useful as it is now. That's fine, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but it's still worth using. I'd tell Carol we did the right thing getting the orders on it. I'd say to anyone starting a small business, use it for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change my life much. I'm still on low pay with a fortnight saved and a room at my aunt's. The thing holding me back from my own hens isn't AI, it's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Ashby's and save fifty a month toward a second-hand mobile shed. I'd ask Carol if I could keep a few hundred of my own hens on her land and sell the eggs at the Saturday market. I'd use the AI to plan the costs and the market stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit impatient. I want to get on with my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a mobile shed cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A second-hand one for three hundred birds is about six thousand. Then the birds, the feed, the fencing. I'd need a small loan, and I don't love the idea of debt, but a business loan for something real is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Carol agree to your hens on her land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if I paid rent and didn't compete with her shops. Carol started with fifty hens in a back garden herself, so she gets it. She'd probably want a cut, which is fair.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold** but still worth using.
I'd tell small businesses to use it for the **boring bits**.
think: My life barely changes, still **low pay** and a room at my aunt's.
**Money**, not AI, holds me back from my own hens.
do: Save **fifty a month** toward a mobile shed.
Ask Carol to let me keep **my own hens** on her land.
Use AI to plan the **Saturday market** stall.
feel: **Fine**, but impatient to start my own thing.
S0.quote: The thing holding me back from my own hens isn't AI, it's money.
fieldNote: Priya is a **daily AI user** who set up the farm's order system.
Her goal is her **own egg business**, blocked by capital.
She accepts **business debt** but not personal borrowing, a traditional distinction.

steps.text: Keep collecting and grading eggs at Ashby's
Save fifty pounds a month toward a mobile hen shed
Sell eggs from her own hens at the Saturday market

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. That's orders, invoices, booking the egg lorry. I already do that with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to learn. I'd tell people to stop moaning and get stuck in. The market will reward people who use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's mostly good. I'm already the AI person at Ashby's, so I'm useful. The only risk is Carol deciding she doesn't need a junior to pack eggs once grading robots get cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small flock on Carol's land in the first year, with a loan for the shed. I'd use AI to run the orders and marketing for my eggs. I'd keep working at Ashby's three or four days while my business grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little uneasy about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ashby's would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who's been packing eggs for fifteen years and hates screens. If the grading gets automated, Gary's the one who goes. I'd try to help Gary learn the new grader, but he's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to the government for help with the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd go to the bank and my family. My uncle lent my cousin money for his van, and my cousin paid it back in a year. That's how it should work.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for anyone willing to learn.
I'd say the **market rewards** people who use the tools.
think: I'm already the **AI person** at Ashby's, so I'm useful.
Cheap **grading robots** could make a junior packer surplus.
do: Start my **own small flock** on Carol's land with a shed loan.
Use AI to run **orders and marketing**.
Keep working at Ashby's **three or four days**.
feel: **Excited**, with some unease about the loan.
S1.quote: My uncle lent my cousin money for his van, and my cousin paid it back in a year.
fieldNote: Priya sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity** for her AI skills.
She'd borrow from **family and the bank**, not government.
She worries for **Gary**, an older packer who avoids screens.

steps.text: Take a bank loan for a second-hand mobile hen shed
Sell eggs from her own flock to village shops
Run her egg orders and marketing on an AI assistant
Keep working three or four days at Ashby's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, AGI. Robots by 2031. That changes the whole sum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and adapt fast, because no one's coming to save them. I'd say families and churches will matter more than ever. I'd not be calling for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking AI in 2028 makes my little egg business easier to run. But robots in 2031 mean big egg farms run cheaper than ever, and my small flock can't compete on price. So I'd have about three years to build a name people pay extra for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my flock straight away, not wait. I'd sell to people who want to know where their eggs come from, a local brand, with my face on the box. I'd save every bit of profit so I'm not in debt when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but determined. Like running for a bus you think you can catch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would people pay extra for your eggs when robot eggs are cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people round here like knowing the farmer. When everything's made by machines, a box of eggs from someone you've met at church means more. That's my bet, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ashby's lets you go before your business is ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd move back in with my parents and work my flock full time. That's what families are for. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say people must **stand** on their **own feet** and adapt fast.
I'd say **families and churches** will matter more than ever.
think: AGI in 2028 makes my **egg business** easier to run.
Robot egg farms in 2031 would **undercut my prices**.
do: Sell a **local brand** with my face on the box.
Save **all profit** to stay debt-free when robots arrive.
feel: **Anxious but determined**, like chasing a bus I can catch.
S2.quote: When everything's made by machines, a box of eggs from someone you've met at church means more.
fieldNote: Priya sees the **three-year gap** as time to build a local brand.
She expects **robot egg farms** to undercut small producers on price.
Her fallback is **family**, moving back in with her parents.

steps.text: Start her own hen flock on Carol's land this year
Save all egg profits to clear the shed loan early
Move back in with her parents if Ashby's lets her go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and robots in 2034. Okay, that's a decent runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to build something real, so people should get on with it. I'd say young people should start businesses now, not wait for jobs. I'd say it at church and in the village group online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years before robots means I can build my flock up to maybe a thousand birds and have a proper name locally. I'd be thirty-five. If the robots come, I'd use them myself, a robot to move the sheds would save my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with three hundred hens and grow each year. I'd use AI for all the orders, the accounts and the marketing. Around 2033, I'd look at buying a robot for my own sheds rather than fearing one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried. I'd be building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a robot. Isn't that the thing that threatens jobs like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot threatens jobs I don't own, but if I own the farm, the robot works for me. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your aunt say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt would say be careful, don't overreach, and go to church on Sunday. She'd also lend me her van for the market. She's like that.

I'd tell young people to **start businesses** now, not wait for jobs.
I'd say it at **church** and in the village group online.
think: I could grow my flock to **a thousand birds** by 2034.
I'd use **robots myself** to move the sheds.
do: Start with **three hundred hens** and grow each year.
Use AI for **orders, accounts and marketing**.
Buy a **robot** for my own sheds around 2033.
S3.quote: A robot threatens jobs I don't own, but if I own the farm, the robot works for me.
fieldNote: Priya's answer to automation is **ownership**: own the farm, own the robot.
She'd scale up to **a thousand birds** over eight years.

steps.text: Grow her flock from three hundred to a thousand hens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. That's honestly the best version for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone who's willing to work. I'd say businesses should grow and hire, and people should learn. I'd say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be forty with my own farm business, if things go right. Robots would be my tools, not my replacement. The only worry is the first few years, getting the loan and not going under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the flock slowly, maybe add a farm shop. I'd save hard in the first years to pay off the shed. I'd keep learning every new AI tool as it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Excited even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a fortnight saved. How can you feel calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got a plan and ten years to do it. Money's tight now, but it's tight for a reason. I'd rather be broke and building than comfortable and stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could knock you off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bird flu, honestly. One outbreak and the flock's gone, robots or no robots. That's a bigger risk to me than AGI.

I'd say businesses should **grow and hire**.
I'd say people should **keep learning**, and say it loudly.
think: By 2039 I could have **my own farm business**.
Robots would be **my tools**, not my replacement.
The only worry is the **loan** in the first few years.
do: Grow the flock slowly and add a **farm shop**.

fieldNote: Priya is **calm** with a decade because the change suits her business plan.

steps.text: Add a farm shop to sell her own eggs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years to build a business that can compete with robot egg farms, with no money behind me. What would help is small business loans for young farmers at fair rates, and less paperwork for starting up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who'll own the farms. If big companies own all the farms and robots, the villages die. If young people own small farms and their own robots, the villages live.

headlineQuote: If young people own small farms and their own robots, the villages live.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old egg farm worker** at Ashby's, a free-range poultry and arable farm.
She uses **AI daily** and set up the farm's ordering system.
Her goal is her **own egg business** on rented land, funded by a loan.
She believes in **ownership and self-reliance** and turns to family before government.
She's **calm** about AGI by 2036 but anxious when robots come by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with three years to build a business before robot egg farms.
whatWouldHelp: Fair **small business loans** for young farmers.
**Less paperwork** for starting a farm business.
